clue.text: Politician reads comic a lot, surprisingly!

indicators.note: surprisingly suggests the letters of the four words before it turn out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A politician confesses, to general amazement, to devouring comics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' rearranges all fourteen letters of READS COMIC A LOT into the two-word party label.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a centre-left party of that name is a kind of politician.

clue.text: Where Maid Marian was second female timber supplier Foster upset

parts.note: her is a female pronoun
a wood is a stand of trees, which supplies timber

indicators.note: upset means the letters of Foster are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A woodman named Foster, whose timber deal soured, is linked to Robin Hood's sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' scrambles FOSTER into the second word. Maid Marian is Robin Hood's companion in English legend, living with him in the Nottinghamshire forest.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend places Robin Hood's outlaw band, Marian included, in this Nottinghamshire woodland.

clue.text: Run-of-the-mill modern groom can dance

indicators.note: to make the words dance is to set their letters moving into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A thoroughly ordinary bridegroom of today turns out to be able to dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dance' rearranges MODERN GROOM CAN into the hyphenated phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe something ordinary and unremarkable, the usual type.

clue.text: All-round banker accepted god

indicators.note: accepted means one piece takes the other inside itself

parts.note: taken as written
a river has banks, so the River Po is a crossword banker
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: A banker who is well-rounded has been welcomed among the gods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepted' puts PO inside ALL, giving APOLL, and the round O follows. 'banker' is a river (something with banks): the Po flows across northern Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek deity of music, poetry and the sun.

clue.text: See 1
Mild oath from aged members

indicators.note: members are parts of a body, so the word aged is broken into its parts and put back in another order

explanation.surface: Elderly club members let slip a gentle curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'members' signals that the four letters of AGED are reassembled into the old exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned exclamation of surprise, a softened form of 'by God'.

clue.text: Big guns rule I overlooked

indicators.note: overlooked means the I is passed over and left out of the word for rule

parts.note: an ordinance is an official rule or decree

explanation.surface: A soldier admits he ignored the rule about heavy artillery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooked' drops the I from ORDINANCE, a rule or decree.
explanation.definitionFit: Military artillery, heavy guns collectively, takes this name.

clue.text: Staffs, in which a Parisian cycles

indicators.note: in which says the French article sits within the word for staffs

parts.note: rods are staffs or sticks
a Parisian says un for the indefinite article a

explanation.surface: Office staff watch a Frenchman pedalling around the building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in which' puts UN, French for 'a', inside RODS. 'Staffs' reads as employees but means sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: Rounds are repeated circuits or sequences, as are cycles.

clue.text: Assuming it's up to me to admit person is dawdling?

indicators.note: to admit means the chain of the other pieces lets the person into it

parts.note: assuming a role is taking it on, so assuming means taking

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters of it's are read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written, losing the apostrophe
taken as written
one is a person, as in 'one should be careful'

explanation.surface: Someone suspects a dawdler's case is down to them to let in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ITS into STI, giving TAKING + STI + ME; 'to admit' lets ONE into that chain after TAKING.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing things slowly and without hurry is the idiom's sense, which suits a dawdler.

clue.text: Divorcee given opportunity retired to West Country area

parts.note: a former spouse is an ex

indicators.note: retired means the word for opportunity goes backwards, withdrawing

parts.note: room means scope or opportunity, as in room for improvement

explanation.surface: A divorced woman, given the chance, retired to the south-west of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' reverses ROOM to MOOR. The West Country is south-west England; this moorland national park lies in Somerset and Devon.
explanation.definitionFit: A national park of upland moor in south-west England, straddling Somerset and Devon.

clue.text: Firm taking advantage of misfortune

parts.note: firm means solid or hard
luck is good fortune, an advantage that comes by chance

explanation.surface: A ruthless company profits from other people's bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' and 'of' only join the pieces: HARD, for firm, takes LUCK.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad luck, an unlucky turn of events, is what the phrase means.

clue.text: "Girls Sam Hunted" is to be broadcast; it's hot stuff!

indicators.note: broadcast scatters things widely, so the letters of the quoted title are spread out and regathered

explanation.surface: A programme called Girls Sam Hunted is going out on air and promises to be steamy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is to be broadcast' rearranges GIRLS SAM HUNTED. 'hot stuff' sounds racy but means a fiery condiment.
explanation.definitionFit: A notably pungent yellow condiment made from ground seeds, so hot in flavour.

clue.text: Forest, it's said, would win

indicators.note: it's said means the phrase is to be heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: would land, as in land a prize, which is to win it

explanation.surface: Someone guesses which forest entry would carry off the prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's said' marks the sound: WOULD LAND, with 'land' meaning win, is heard as the word for wooded country.
explanation.definitionFit: Land covered with trees is a forest.

clue.text: See 2
See 11
Musician ought to be going round job centre

parts.note: ought is an old word for nought, zero, so the letter O

indicators.note: going round means the verb encircles the next piece

parts.note: be is the verb 'to be'

indicators.note: centre picks the middle letter of the word job

explanation.surface: A player ought to be visiting the job centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' puts O, the middle of JOB, inside BE, after O for ought (zero). A job centre is a British state employment office.
explanation.definitionFit: In orchestral usage the instrument's name stands for its player, as in 'second oboe'.

clue.text: Ruffle fellow with clue on running

indicators.note: running means the letters of clue on are set in motion and rearranged

explanation.surface: A man with a lead in a race gets himself ruffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running' rearranges CLUE ON into LOUNCE, after F for fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: A flounce is a frill or ruffle of fabric on a garment.

clue.text: Disappears with vehicle is she inside it?

parts.note: a van is a vehicle

indicators.note: inside says she is put within the word is that the clue calls it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A van drives off; the question is whether the woman is in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts SHE within IS, giving I-SHE-S, after VAN; 'it' points back to 'is', not to the van.
explanation.definitionFit: To vanish is to disappear from sight.

clue.text: Figure these words will follow

parts.note: the clue's own words come straight after its number in the printed list, so the figure they follow is that number

explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes its own position: it is the down clue numbered with this figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The number printed beside this clue is a figure, and the clue's words come after it.

clue.text: See 8
Change seat in university

indicators.note: in means the word for seat goes into the word for change

parts.note: to vary is to change
to seat oneself is to sit

explanation.surface: A student swaps chairs at college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts SIT inside VARY. The answer is the British informal word for a university, seen in the Oxford-Cambridge Varsity Match.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British name for a university, especially in sport.

clue.text: Some chaps and I put in an appearance

indicators.note: put in means the I is placed inside the word for chaps

parts.note: chaps are men

explanation.surface: A few blokes and I show up at the event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put in' sets I inside MEN. 'put in an appearance' looks like a single idiom, but 'appearance' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's mien is their look or bearing.

clue.text: See 1 down
Topless weirdo follows street band

indicators.note: topless means the top letter of the word for weirdo is removed

parts.note: a freak is a weirdo

explanation.surface: A strange topless figure trails a street musician group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' strips the F from FREAK, and 'follows' places the remainder after ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A streak is a stripe or band of colour.

clue.text: Book a nun's written about Jolson

indicators.note: about means the letters of nun are turned around into a fresh order

parts.note: the nun, losing the possessive
Al Jolson was the American singer of The Jazz Singer

explanation.surface: A nun has penned a book about a famous singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges NUN to NNU; 'written' is a link. Al Jolson was an American singer and actor.
explanation.definitionFit: An annual is a book issued yearly, often a children's gift edition.

clue.text: Not allowed to attack gang

parts.note: out means not permitted, as in smoking is out
a fit is an attack, as of coughing

explanation.surface: Gang members are told they may not launch an assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attack' is a noun here, a sudden bout.
explanation.definitionFit: An outfit is a group or organisation, informally a gang.

clue.text: Shoots supporter inches away with one

parts.note: a bra is an item of support underwear

indicators.note: away with means the one is removed from inches

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A support is fitted inches away while someone fires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'away with' removes I (one) from INCHES, leaving NCHES after BRA. 'Shoots' is a noun, new plant growth.
explanation.definitionFit: New growth on a tree, its shoots, forms its branches.

clue.text: Home, to a companion, is a small island

parts.note: being in is being at home
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A companion is told the cottage is on a tiny isle.
explanation.walkthrough: CH is Companion of Honour, a British honour. In Scotland and Ireland the word means a small island.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish and Irish word for an islet, as in Inchcolm.

clue.text: Emirate starts to plan the new jumbo

indicators.note: starts means the opening letter of Emirate is taken and leads off the answer
new means plan the is made afresh in a different order

explanation.surface: A Gulf state begins planning a new jumbo jet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' gives E, and 'new' rearranges PLAN THE into LEPHANT. 'jumbo' suggests an airliner but means the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Jumbo was a famous zoo elephant, and the name became a byword for the animal.

clue.text: Smell, when coming back about one, bones

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell

indicators.note: coming back means the word for about is read in reverse

parts.note: re means about or concerning
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A smell returns around the joint of meat on the bone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming back' turns RE into ER; 'when' is a link. In British slang a 'hum' is a stink.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the upper-arm bones, plural of the Latin name for that bone.

clue.text: Given gentle push Kate recklessly gets married!

indicators.note: recklessly suggests the letters of gentle push Kate are thrown together carelessly in a new order

explanation.surface: After a little nudge, Kate rushes into marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recklessly' rearranges GENTLE PUSH KATE into the idiom; 'Given' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means committing to a bold step, often used of deciding to wed.
